interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the bold sum arrow's height always equal to the two arrows' heights stacked, so its wave is the two waves added, when you pause the two arrows turning together.
interactive.title: Two arrows, one sum
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens, most on one picture, two arrows and their sum. At the top, arrow A (solid ink) and arrow B (dashed ink) turn anticlockwise together at one steady speed, as From circle to wave's arm did. B is drawn with its tail on A's tip, tip to tail, and a bold arrow runs from the centre to B's tip: the sum arrow. Below, three waves are traced against time from the arrows' heights: A's wave, B's wave and the bold sum wave. The rule is From circle to wave's: each wave's height at any instant is its arrow's height, length × sin of its angle. Because B starts on A's tip, B's tip is B's height above A's tip, so the sum arrow's height is always A's height plus B's height. A pause button freezes the picture, and two bars, A's height and B's height, stack beside the wave graph to the sum's height. On screens that show an idea, sliders set each arrow's length (1 to 10) and starting angle (−180° to 180°); a shadows switch splits each arrow into its floor shadow and wall shadow, as in Finding angles, with the sums of the shadows read out; a speed switch makes B turn twice as fast as A. Screen 1 starts A 3 long pointing right and B 4 long a quarter turn on: they make a right-angled triangle, so the sum arrow is √(3² + 4²) = 5 long at tan⁻¹(4 ÷ 3) = 53.1°, and the sum wave peaks at 5. Screen 2 asks for that peak: 5, 7 (the lengths added) or 1 (one taken from the other). Screen 3 sets A to 10 at 0° and B to 6 at 60° with the shadows switch on: B's floor shadow is 6 cos 60° = 3 and its wall shadow 6 sin 60° = 5.196, the floor shadows add to 13 and the wall shadows to 5.196, so the sum is √(13² + 5.196²) = 14 long, and its wave peaks at 14, not 16. Screen 4 asks the length of 4 at 0° plus 4 at 60°: 6.93 (floor 4 + 2 = 6, wall 3.464, √48), 8 (the lengths added) or 4 (the cosine rule with 60° where the triangle's angle is 120°). Screen 5 marks the sum's angle, tan⁻¹(5.196 ÷ 13) = 21.8°, between A's and B's, writes the sum wave as 14 sin(ωt + 21.8°), and checks the length by the cosine rule: inside the tip-to-tail triangle the angle at B's tail is 180° − 60° = 120°, and 10² + 6² − 2 × 10 × 6 × cos 120° = 196 = 14². Screen 6 asks the angle of 4 at 0° plus 4 at 60°: 30° (tan⁻¹(3.464 ÷ 6)), 60° (B's own angle) or 0.577 (the ratio, with tan⁻¹ left out). Screen 7 takes B away from A: B's arrow turns half a turn, to 240°, and is added, giving floor 10 − 3 = 7, wall −5.196 and a difference 8.72 long at −36.6°. Screen 8 is the three-phase card, drawn to its own scale in volts: three arrows L1, L2 and L3, each 230 V long and a third of a turn, 120°, apart, drawn at the rms value, 230 V, as a label says; at peak each would be 325.3 V and the line arrow 563.4 V, the same shape √2 times bigger. L2 sits a third of a turn behind L1. Each line's voltage is measured from neutral, so a meter across L1 and L2 reads one minus the other, L1 − L2, and L2 turns half a turn and is added to L1: floor 230 + 115 = 345, wall 199.2, a line arrow 398.4 long, 30° ahead of L1. A line down the middle of that triangle halves it into two right-angled triangles with 60° at the centre, so the line voltage is 2 × 230 × sin 60° = 230 × √3. It is step 4's answer, 6.93 = 4 × √3, drawn bigger. Screen 9 asks what the meter reads: 398 V, 460 V (230 + 230) or 230 V (one phase's arrow). Screen 10 turns the speed switch on: the angle between A and B now keeps changing, so the tip-to-tail triangle changes shape, the sum arrow stretches and shrinks as it turns, and the sum wave is no longer one clean sine wave. Screen 11 asks what the sum arrow does with B turning twice as fast: keeps changing length, so the sum is no single sine wave; keeps its length and turns one and a half times as fast; or stays as it was. Screens 12, 13 and 14 are mixed. Screen 12: a college's marine notes say most ships have a three-phase 440 V supply, 440 V between lines; is each phase-to-neutral voltage 254 V (440 ÷ √3), 220 V (halved) or 762 V (440 × √3)? Screen 13: 8 sin ωt plus 8 sin(ωt + 180°); is the sum's peak 0 (the arrows point opposite ways, so B's tip comes back to the centre and the waves cancel), 16 (the lengths added) or 11.3 (√(8² + 8²), as if a quarter turn apart)? Screen 14: two branch currents, 12 A peak in step with the supply and 5 A peak a quarter turn behind it, join: is the supply current 13 A peak lagging by 22.6°, 17 A (the sizes added), or 13 A leading by 22.6° (the minus sign of the wall shadow dropped)? Each puzzle offers three answers; a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the answer on the picture. The last Why? and the closing line add that the floor shadow and wall shadow of an arrow are what Complex numbers writes as one number.
interactive.ignores: The arrows turn far more slowly than a real 50 Hz supply, which turns fifty times a second, so you can watch the heights stack. The waves are perfect sine waves; real supply voltages are close to this shape but not exactly it. The three-phase card draws three exactly equal arrows exactly 120° apart; a real supply's phases are very close to that but not exact. Arrow lengths, angles and currents in the puzzles are example figures, and readouts are rounded while the working keeps every figure.

explain.text:
Two waves of the same frequency, added instant by instant, make a third wave of that same frequency (unless they cancel exactly), and you can find it without drawing a single wave. Draw each wave's turning arrow, lay the second arrow's tail on the first arrow's tip, and the arrow from the start of the first to the tip of the second is the sum's arrow: its length is the sum's peak and its angle is the sum's phase.

Remember From circle to wave: a wave's height at any instant is the height of its turning arrow's tip. Lay arrow B's tail on arrow A's tip, and B's tip sits B's height above A's tip, so the end of the chain is at A's height plus B's height. The sum arrow, from the centre to that end, therefore has the two heights added at every instant: the sum of the up parts of the separate arrows is the up part of the sum arrow.[^5] Both arrows turn at the same speed, so the angle between them never changes, and the chain turns as one rigid shape, like a bent bar spun about one end. The sum arrow keeps its length and turns at the same speed, so its height traces a sine wave of the same frequency, which is why phasors are good for summing sine waves of one frequency.[^6] Textbooks call each turning arrow a [[phasor]] and draw it frozen at the instant t = 0, because the whole picture just turns from there.

To measure the sum arrow, split each arrow as you split a force in Finding angles: the cosine gives the floor shadow and the sine the wall shadow,[^7] so an arrow of length E at angle θ has floor shadow E cos θ and wall shadow E sin θ. Floor shadows add along the floor and wall shadows up the wall; then Pythagoras gives the sum's length and inverse tan its angle. Take 10 sin ωt plus 6 sin(ωt + 60°). Arrow A is 10 along the floor. Arrow B has floor shadow 6 cos 60° = 3 and wall shadow 6 sin 60° = 5.196. The sum has floor shadow 13 and wall shadow 5.196, so its length is √(13² + 5.196²) = 14 and its angle is tan⁻¹(5.196 ÷ 13) = 21.8°: the sum is 14 sin(ωt + 21.8°). It peaks at 14, not 16, because A and B reach their peaks at different moments. The cosine rule from Triangles without a right angle checks it: inside the tip-to-tail triangle the angle between the arrows is 180° − 60° = 120°, and 10² + 6² − 2 × 10 × 6 × cos 120° = 196 = 14².[^8] Textbooks add that an arrow further round anticlockwise is said to lead and one behind to be [[lagging]]: here the sum leads A by 21.8°. Taking a wave away is adding its arrow turned half a turn, because an arm half a turn on has every height with its sign changed.

That answers the course's puzzle. A three-phase supply's three voltages are equal in size and 120° apart,[^1] and in the UK each is declared at 230 V between phase and neutral.[^2] UK mains voltages are rms values,[^9] so this triangle is drawn at rms; at peak every side is √2 times longer and the shape is the same. Each line's voltage is measured from neutral, so a meter across two lines reads one minus the other, the [[line voltage]], whose arrow joins the two phase arrows' tips. In the triangle made by the two phase arrows and that line, a line from the centre down the middle halves it into two right-angled triangles with 60° at the centre (the screen draws the same triangle tip to tail, so its halving line runs from L1's tip, with 60° each side of it there), so the line voltage is 2 × 230 × sin 60° = 230 × √3 = 398 V, not 460 V: about 400 V, the figure low-voltage supplies are described by alongside 230 V single-phase.[^3] √3 is the multiplier that comes with the 30° shift between a star supply's line and phase voltages.[^10] Two cautions. Waves of different frequencies cannot share one phasor diagram, because their arrows turn at different speeds;[^11] the angle between them keeps changing, so no single steady arrow stands for their sum. And texts differ over the arrow's length: Electronics Tutorials gives a phasor the rms value of its wave and a vector the peak,[^12] while UNSW's Physclips says phasor diagrams drawn at rms have the same shape as those drawn at the peak, scaled by 0.71.[^4] Use one or the other throughout a diagram, never both. These are ideal sine waves, a simplified model; real supply waves are close to sine waves but not exactly. **Two waves of one frequency add by putting their phasors tip to tail: the arrow from start to finish is the sum, its length the peak and its angle the phase.[^6]**

analogy.text: Two winch ropes pull on one shackle, say 10 kN along the deck and 6 kN at 60° to it. Lay one pull's arrow on the end of the other and the shackle feels a single pull of 14 kN at 21.8° to the first rope, not 16 kN, because the ropes pull partly across each other. Adding phasors is the same drawing.
analogy.breaks: The rope pulls stand still and are real pushes and pulls. Phasors turn, and only their heights, read at one instant, are the waves' values; the arrows themselves are a way of keeping count. Waves of different frequencies have no rope picture at all, because their arrows do not keep the same angle.

practice.text:
The MCA's Marine Electro-technology syllabus asks you to explain phasors and to solve problems adding and subtracting ac voltages and currents by the phasor method.[^13]

- Check that every wave has the same frequency. If not, phasors cannot add them.
- Pick peak or rms for every arrow, and keep to it.
- Draw each arrow at t = 0: its length the wave's peak (or rms), its angle the wave's phase, anticlockwise counted positive.
- To take a wave away, turn its arrow half a turn (add 180°) and add it.
- Split each arrow: floor shadow E cos θ, wall shadow E sin θ, keeping their signs.
- Add the floor shadows; add the wall shadows.
- The sum's length is √(floor² + wall²) and its angle is tan⁻¹(wall ÷ floor), plus 180° if the floor total is negative.
- Check: the sum is no longer than the two lengths added, and no shorter than one taken from the other. For two arrows, the cosine rule with the angle inside the triangle, 180° minus the angle between them, gives the same length.

**Rule of thumb:** For three equal phases 120° apart, each phase measured to neutral (a star supply), the line voltage is the phase voltage × √3, about 1.732, and the phase voltage is the line voltage ÷ √3. So 230 V a phase gives 398 V between lines, described as 400 V,[^3] and a ship's 440 V line voltage, which a college's marine notes say most ships have,[^14] means 254 V a phase.

**Worked example:** Two voltages in series, say 100 V peak and 50 V peak 30° ahead of it. Arrow A: floor 100, wall 0. Arrow B: floor 50 cos 30° = 43.3, wall 50 sin 30° = 25. Totals: floor 143.3, wall 25. The sum is √(143.3² + 25²) = 145.5 V peak at tan⁻¹(25 ÷ 143.3) = 9.9° ahead of A. Check by the cosine rule with 180° − 30° = 150°: √(100² + 50² − 2 × 100 × 50 × cos 150°) = 145.5. Not 150 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the sizes: 230 V + 230 V = 460 V. Sizes add only when the arrows point the same way.
- Putting waves of different frequencies on one diagram.
- Mixing peak and rms arrows on one diagram.
- Using the angle between the arrows in the cosine rule, instead of 180° minus it.
- Dropping the minus sign of a wall shadow, so a sum that lags is read as leading.
- Trusting the calculator's tan⁻¹ when the floor total is negative: the sum then points left, so add 180°.

Complex numbers, the next course, writes an arrow's floor shadow and wall shadow as one number, so adding phasors becomes adding numbers.
